title: Reading a mishnah
hookLine: a case, a few opinions, and often an anonymous ruling

lines: SONS HOME LATE FROM A WEDDING.
cards: From what time may the Shema be recited in the evening? That's the question that opens the tractate Berakhot. Not why.
Not whether. When. And the answer doesn't come in one voice.
It comes as a small crowd: Rabbi Eliezer, then the Sages, then Rabban Gamliel. And then, as if the page can't help itself, a story about Rabban Gamliel's sons coming home late from a wedding.
You met this mishnah back in year one. Now, with the six orders behind you, here's how to read it.

teach.h: THE CASE: FROM THE PRIESTS' MEAL.
teach.b: Reading a mishnah. Four moves. First, the case.
A mishnah tends to start with a concrete question, and this one answers with a picture, not a clock: from the hour the priests go in to eat their holy portion.
Those are priests who were impure, who immersed, and who waited for evening. Water and time, from the last few days, become the start of the evening prayer.
Second, the voices. Until when? Rabbi Eliezer says, until the end of the first watch of the night.
The Sages say, until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says, until dawn rises. Three answers, each with a name, and the Mishnah keeps all three.
Third, the story. Rabban Gamliel's sons come home from a wedding feast and tell him they haven't said the Shema. He tells them: if dawn hasn't risen, you are still obliged to say it.
Then the Mishnah explains the Sages' midnight: they set it as a fence, to keep people far from missing it. So the stricter voice turns out to be a guardrail, not a different law.

teach.h: STAM: THE VOICE WITH NO NAME.
teach.b: Fourth, the voice with no name. Here no one argues over the start; the debate is only about the end. In other mishnahs a ruling is given with no name at all.
A line like that is called stam, plain. The Talmud has a saying that an unnamed mishnah is Rabbi Meir's, and readers learn to listen hard for that plain voice.
So: find the case, hear each voice by name, watch for a story, then listen for who speaks without a name.

how: Jews who study Mishnah sometimes learn it with a partner or in a class, reading each mishnah aloud, naming its case and its voices, and some study a set amount each day.

games.q: you're Rabban Gamliel's son, home from a wedding feast after midnight, and you haven't said the evening Shema. you ask your father. what does he say?
o: too late. the Sages said midnight.
if dawn hasn't risen, you still have to say it.
skip it and say it twice tomorrow.
games.why: he tells them: if dawn hasn't risen, you are obliged to say it. the Mishnah then explains the Sages' midnight as a fence.

practice: Take the mishnah you just heard and say its question to yourself: from what time, until what time? Let each voice speak in turn, Rabbi Eliezer, the Sages, Rabban Gamliel, and picture the sons at the door, late and a little worried.
Notice which voice you lean toward, and that the page never makes you choose.
